conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in caring for new mothers and the emotional changes that can show up after a baby arrives.  

Right now I’m going to guide you through a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share is confidential and safe in this room.  

Once we’re finished, we’ll look at your responses together and decide what kind of support—if any—might be most helpful for you right now.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin with the first question.  

**Question 1**  
Looking back over the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things? Some new moms find themselves laughing easily, some notice it’s harder than before, and others fall somewhere in-between. What’s it been like for you lately?

Honestly, I’ve still been able to laugh, but it feels… dimmed. Like I’ll chuckle at something silly my husband says or when the baby makes a funny face, but the laughter fades fast and it doesn’t feel as bright as it used to. I’d say maybe half the time I can still find the funny side—other times I’m just too tired or preoccupied.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes, but not as easily as before the baby. I’ll manage a quick laugh, yet it feels kind of forced—like I’m doing it because I know I should, not because it comes naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some things—like my morning coffee or when my mom comes over to hold the baby so I can shower—but the excitement feels pretty muted. It’s more “oh, that’ll be nice” than the real spark I used to feel.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Like when the baby spit up a lot after feeding, I kept thinking I must’ve eaten something that upset him. And the other night he wouldn’t settle, and I caught myself wondering if I’m just not doing something right. I know, rationally, babies just fuss, but the thought still pops up that it’s somehow my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah. I’ll be sitting there while the baby’s napping and suddenly feel this knot in my chest—like something bad is about to happen—even though everything looks fine. I keep checking to make sure he’s breathing or worrying that a tiny cough means he’s getting sick, even when there’s no real sign.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-blown panic, but a couple of times I’ve had this sudden rush of “what if I can’t handle this?” while I’m just feeding him or folding laundry. My heart races, I feel shaky, and I have to remind myself to breathe. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—some days it feels like the minute I finish one thing, two more pile on. I’ll finally get the baby down and realize the bottles need sterilizing, the laundry’s overflowing, and I haven’t eaten. I end up standing in the kitchen just staring, not sure what to tackle first.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—more like wired and overwhelmed. A few nights this week I’ve lain down exhausted, but my brain keeps spinning through to-do lists and “what-ifs” about the baby. It takes me maybe an hour to drift off, and then I’m up again when he wakes.
I have felt sad or miserable

Off and on, yeah. Not every moment, but it hits in waves—like when I’m rocking the baby at 3 a.m. and suddenly feel this heaviness. It usually lifts once the sun’s up and I see him smile, but those low patches feel pretty deep while they last.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Only once this week. It was the night he wouldn’t settle for almost two hours—my husband had to take over while I went in the bathroom and just teared up for a minute. Mostly I feel teary, but I manage to hold it back.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that the joy of new motherhood feels dimmed-laughter comes out forced, excitement is muted, and waves of heaviness catch you in the quiet hours. Between constant worry that something will go wrong, racing thoughts that keep you awake, and guilt over everyday baby hiccups, you're feeling overwhelmed and stretched thin, though you're relieved you've had no thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports reduced ability to laugh, describing it as forced and unnatural, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeably diminished enjoyment and anticipation, matching 'Definitely less than I used to</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "a few times this week" with specific examples, aligning with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily unexpected anxiety spikes and persistent intrusive worries without objective cause, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden unexpected anxiety episodes with physical panic-like symptoms (racing heart, shaking, breathlessness) occurring repeatedly, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes clear sleep disruption linked to anxious racing thoughts, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges recurring sadness that comes "in waves" and feels "deep" during night-time, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 18 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression. Your answers describe the past-week presence of <sym>depressed mood</sym>, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), inappropriate guilt, psychomotor agitation (racing heart, shakes), sleep disruption not solely due to infant care, and difficulty coping-all criteria aligning with <med>DSM-5 Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> to review results and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based supports such as <med>CBT for postpartum depression</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Schedule an appointment with our practice's <med>postpartum support group</med> within the next two weeks
4. Implement brief daily self-check-ins using the EPDS questions; if score remains above 12 or Q10 ≥1, seek same-day help
5. Enlist partner/family for rotating night shifts so you can obtain a minimum 4-hour stretch of uninterrupted sleep
6. Practice 5-minute grounding or paced-breathing exercises when you feel the sudden rush of panic
7. Plan a follow-up EPDS screening in two weeks to monitor progress after supports are in place
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood/Anxiety (self-report, EPDS-style items)

Presenting symptoms  
- Anhedonia & reduced pleasure: laughter feels forced, anticipatory enjoyment “muted”  
- Persistent low/sad mood: “waves of heaviness,” especially at night  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame over routine infant care  
- Unwarranted anxiety and episodic panic sensations (physical arousal, “what-ifs,” repeated checking on baby)  
- Overwhelm and difficulty managing daily tasks  
- Initial insomnia secondary to racing thoughts; not purely infant-driven awakenings  
- One crying episode this week; frequent tearfulness suppressed  

Pattern  
Mood and anxiety symptoms present most days, worst in evening/night, with partial daytime relief when infant smiles or support is available.

Screening significance  
Responses are consistent with mild–moderate postpartum depression with prominent anxiety; meet threshold for further evaluation (likely EPDS ≥ 10–12 range).

Risk factors noted  
- Depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, sleep disruption linked to mood, anxiety/panic, sense of being overwhelmed  
- NO self-harm ideation reported → acute safety risk absent at time of screen

Plan  
Recommend formal EPDS scoring, clinical interview for major depression and anxiety disorders, psychoeducation, and discussion of support/intervention options.
